meta.title: Web3Bridge Web3 Knowledge Assessment - Part 1

types.mcq: single correct option; 'answer' is a 0-based index
types.multi: select all that apply; 'answer' is an array of 0-based indices; award full points only on exact match
types.open: written answer, graded manually by the instructor using 'rubric'

meta.note: SERVER-SIDE ONLY: 'answer', 'explanation' and 'rubric' must never be sent to the student's browser during the exam.

questions.question: What is the key difference between an EOA and a contract account?
options: Contract accounts are controlled by private keys; EOAs are controlled by code
EOAs are controlled by private keys; contract accounts are controlled by their deployed code
Only contract accounts have a nonce
questions.explanation: EOAs are controlled by a private key. Contract accounts have no key and execute code when called.

questions.question: Which consensus mechanism does Ethereum use after the Merge?
questions.explanation: Ethereum moved from PoW to PoS in September 2022.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the account nonce?
options: Ensuring each transaction from an account is processed once and in order
questions.explanation: The nonce counts transactions from an account, preventing replays and enforcing ordering.

questions.question: Why can't a smart contract call an external web API directly?
options: Solidity has no syntax for it
Every node must reproduce the same deterministic result, and external data may differ between nodes and times
APIs are too expensive in gas
questions.explanation: Consensus requires determinism. Oracles bring off-chain data on-chain via transactions.

questions.question: After EIP-1559, what happens to the base fee?
options: It is paid to the validator
It is sent to a treasury
It is refunded to the sender
questions.explanation: The base fee is burned; only the priority fee (tip) goes to the validator.

questions.question: How is an Ethereum address derived from a key pair?
options: Last 20 bytes of the keccak256 hash of the public key
First 20 bytes of the SHA-256 of the private key
Base58 encoding of the public key
questions.explanation: address = last 20 bytes of keccak256(publicKey).

questions.question: How many bytes is an Ethereum address?
questions.explanation: 20 bytes (160 bits), shown as 40 hex characters.

questions.question: What does 'finality' mean on Ethereum?
options: The transaction is in the mempool
A block cannot be reverted without a large amount of stake being destroyed (slashed)
The transaction has exactly one confirmation
questions.explanation: Finalized blocks are economically irreversible under PoS.

questions.question: How do optimistic rollups differ from ZK rollups?
options: Optimistic rollups assume transactions are valid and rely on fraud proofs during a challenge window; ZK rollups post validity proofs
ZK rollups use fraud proofs; optimistic rollups use validity proofs
Optimistic rollups do not post any data to L1
questions.explanation: Optimistic = fraud proofs and a challenge period. ZK = cryptographic validity proofs.

questions.question: What is the mempool?
options: A pool of pending transactions waiting to be included in a block
questions.explanation: Pending transactions sit in the mempool until a block builder includes them.

questions.question: Which is NOT a property of a cryptographic hash function?
options: A small input change drastically changes the output
questions.explanation: Hashes are one-way.

questions.question: Select ALL that can change Ethereum state.
options: A signed transaction from an EOA
An eth_call to a view function
A contract calling another contract inside a transaction
questions.explanation: eth_call is a local simulation and never changes state.

questions.question: For an external function taking a large read-only array parameter, which data location is usually cheapest?
questions.explanation: calldata avoids copying the data into memory.

questions.question: Which data location persists between transactions?
questions.explanation: Only storage is persistent contract state.

questions.question: Roughly how much gas does writing a non-zero value to a previously zero storage slot cost (SSTORE)?
questions.explanation: About 20,000 gas (plus 2,100 if the slot is cold).

questions.question: When can a view function still cost gas?
options: When it is called by another contract during a transaction
Only when it returns an array
questions.explanation: Called externally off-chain it is free, but inside a transaction its execution consumes gas.

questions.question: What is the EVM's native word size?
questions.explanation: The EVM is a 256-bit word machine.

questions.question: An EOA calls contract A, A calls B, B calls C. Inside C, what is msg.sender?
questions.explanation: msg.sender is the immediate caller, which is B.

questions.question: In the same call chain (EOA -> A -> B -> C), what is tx.origin inside C?
questions.explanation: tx.origin is always the EOA that started the transaction.

questions.question: What does delegatecall do?
options: Runs the callee's code in the callee's own storage
Runs the callee's code in the caller's storage context, preserving msg.sender and msg.value
questions.explanation: delegatecall borrows the code but uses the caller's storage. This is the basis of proxies.

questions.question: What does staticcall guarantee?
options: The call reverts if the callee tries to modify state
The call uses the caller's storage
questions.explanation: staticcall forbids state changes in the callee, which is how view calls to other contracts are enforced.

questions.question: What is the maximum deployed contract size (EIP-170)?
questions.explanation: 24,576 bytes.

questions.question: How is a function selector computed?
options: First 4 bytes of keccak256 of the function signature
Last 4 bytes of SHA-256 of the function name
First 4 bytes of the contract address
The function's index in the ABI
questions.explanation: e.g. bytes4(keccak256("transfer(address,uint256)")) = 0xa9059cbb.

questions.question: How many storage slots do structs A and B use?
questions.code:
struct A { uint128 a; uint256 b; uint128 c; }
struct B { uint128 a; uint128 c; uint256 b; }
questions.explanation: In A, the two uint128 values are separated by a uint256, so no packing (3 slots). In B, the two uint128 values pack together (2 slots).

questions.question: What does EIP-2929 change about gas costs?
options: First access to a storage slot or address in a transaction costs more than later (warm) accesses
Warm accesses cost more than cold accesses
There is no difference between them
questions.explanation: Cold access is 2,100 gas for slots and 2,600 for addresses, versus about 100 when warm.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of EIP-4844 (blobs)?
options: Provide cheaper temporary data availability for rollups
questions.explanation: Blobs make posting L2 data to L1 much cheaper.

questions.question: What happens if a transaction runs out of gas?
options: All state changes revert and the gas consumed is still paid
questions.explanation: Execution reverts but the validator is still paid for the work done.

questions.question: What is the difference between public and external functions?
options: public can be called internally and externally; external only from outside the contract
external is always cheaper in every case
questions.explanation: external functions cannot be called internally without this.f().

questions.question: In Solidity 0.8+, what happens on arithmetic overflow by default?
options: It reverts with a Panic error
questions.explanation: Checked arithmetic is the default since 0.8.0.

questions.question: What does an unchecked { } block do?
options: Disables overflow/underflow checks inside the block to save gas
questions.explanation: Use only when overflow is provably impossible.

questions.question: How do constant and immutable differ?
options: constant is fixed at compile time; immutable is set once in the constructor
constant is set in the constructor
immutable values live in a mutable storage slot
questions.explanation: Both avoid storage reads; immutable values are embedded in the runtime bytecode at deployment.

questions.question: What happens when a require() fails?
options: State changes revert and remaining gas is refunded to the caller
questions.explanation: require reverts and returns unused gas.

questions.question: Why prefer custom errors over require strings?
options: They are cheaper in gas and can carry typed parameters
questions.explanation: Custom errors encode only a 4-byte selector plus args.

questions.question: How many parameters of an event can be indexed?
questions.explanation: Up to 3 indexed parameters for non-anonymous events.

questions.question: Can you iterate over a Solidity mapping?
options: No, keys are not stored; you need a separate array or EnumerableSet
questions.explanation: Mappings are hash lookups with no key list.

questions.question: What does bump() do to users[msg.sender].balance?
options: Nothing, because u is a memory copy
questions.explanation: Use `User storage u` to modify the stored struct.

questions.question: What happens if you send 1 ETH with a call to buy()?
options: It reverts because buy() is not payable
It is stored only in msg.value
questions.explanation: Non-payable functions reject ETH.

questions.question: A contract has both receive() and fallback(). A plain ETH transfer with empty calldata arrives. Which runs?
questions.explanation: receive handles empty calldata with ETH. fallback handles unmatched selectors.

questions.question: How does an interface differ from an abstract contract?
options: Interfaces cannot have state variables or implemented functions; abstract contracts can
questions.explanation: Interfaces are pure declarations.

questions.question: What happens when you call pop() on an empty storage array?
questions.explanation: Panic(0x31) since 0.8.x.

questions.question: Solidity has no floating point. How do you represent 1.5 tokens with 18 decimals?
Why is transfer()/send() for sending ETH discouraged?
options: The fixed 2300 gas stipend can break with recipients that need more gas
questions.explanation: Gas repricing can break them. Prefer call with a checked result and reentrancy protection.

questions.question: When does a constructor run?
questions.explanation: Constructor code is not part of the runtime bytecode.

questions.question: In a modifier, what does `_;` represent?
options: Where the modified function's body is inserted
questions.explanation: Code before `_;` runs first, then the function body, then the code after.

questions.question: To override a base contract function, what is required?
options: Base function marked virtual and derived function marked override
questions.explanation: Both keywords are required since 0.6.

questions.question: What does f() return?
questions.explanation: Inside unchecked the value wraps to 0.

questions.question: Select ALL valid data locations for reference-type function parameters.
questions.explanation: The stack is not a selectable data location for reference types.

questions.question: In a constant-product AMM (x * y = k), how is price determined?
options: By the ratio of reserves after the trade keeps x * y constant
questions.explanation: Larger trades move the price more.

questions.question: What is impermanent loss?
options: The value difference between providing liquidity and simply holding, caused by price divergence
questions.explanation: It becomes permanent if you withdraw while prices are diverged.

questions.question: What is slippage?
options: The difference between expected and executed price
questions.explanation: Set minAmountOut to bound it.

questions.question: A pool holds 100 ETH and 200,000 USDC (x*y=k, no fees). Roughly how much USDC does it cost to buy 10 ETH?
Why are most DeFi loans over-collateralized?
options: No on-chain identity or credit history, and collateral is volatile, so it must cover the debt
questions.explanation: Over-collateralization protects the lender.

questions.question: What happens when a borrower's health factor drops below 1?
options: Their collateral can be liquidated to repay the debt
questions.explanation: Liquidators repay debt and receive collateral at a discount.

questions.question: Select ALL valid stablecoin designs.
questions.explanation: PoW-backed is not a stablecoin design.

questions.question: How do APR and APY differ?
options: APY includes compounding; APR does not
APR includes compounding; APY does not
questions.explanation: APY reflects reinvested earnings.

questions.question: Why do DAOs use a timelock on governance actions?
options: To delay execution so users can review and exit if they disagree
questions.explanation: It is a safeguard against malicious or rushed proposals.

questions.question: Why are cross-chain bridges frequent hack targets?
options: They hold large pools of locked funds behind complex trust and verification assumptions
questions.explanation: Ronin and Wormhole are well-known examples.

questions.question: What does a decentralized oracle network like Chainlink do?
options: Aggregates off-chain data and delivers it on-chain
questions.explanation: Multiple nodes reduce single points of failure.

questions.question: What do LP tokens represent?
options: A liquidity provider's share of a pool
questions.explanation: Burn LP tokens to redeem your share of the pool plus fees.

questions.question: Select ALL functions that are part of the ERC-20 standard.
questions.explanation: ownerOf belongs to ERC-721.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of ERC-1155 over ERC-721?
options: Multiple token types (fungible and non-fungible) in one contract, with batch operations
It supports batch and 721 does not exist
questions.explanation: ERC-1155 is efficient for games and large collections.

questions.question: USDC uses 6 decimals. How many base units is 1 USDC?
questions.explanation: 1 USDC = 10^6 base units.

questions.question: What does ERC-721's safeTransferFrom do differently from transferFrom?
options: Checks that a receiving contract implements onERC721Received
questions.explanation: It prevents NFTs from getting stuck in contracts that can't handle them.

questions.question: What does ERC-2612 permit enable?
options: Approvals via an off-chain signature, avoiding a separate approve transaction
questions.explanation: The user signs and the spender submits the signature.

questions.question: What is ERC-165 used for?
questions.explanation: It lets other contracts query which interfaces a contract supports.

questions.question: What is special about IPFS addresses (CIDs) for NFT metadata?
options: They are content-addressed, so the CID changes if the content changes
questions.explanation: That makes IPFS content tamper-evident.

questions.question: Alice approved a DEX router for 100 tokens. Who calls transferFrom(alice, pool, 100)?
questions.explanation: The spender calls transferFrom using its allowance.

questions.question: Which command runs Foundry tests?
questions.explanation: forge test compiles and runs Solidity tests.

questions.question: What is fork testing?
options: Running tests against a local copy of live chain state
questions.explanation: It lets you test against real protocols like Uniswap or Aave.

questions.question: What does Foundry's vm.prank(addr) do?
options: Sets msg.sender to addr for the next call
questions.explanation: vm.startPrank persists for multiple calls.

questions.question: In ethers.js, what is the difference between a Provider and a Signer?
options: A Provider reads chain data; a Signer signs and sends transactions
questions.explanation: Provider = read connection. Signer = account that can authorize writes.

questions.question: What does signing a message with a wallet prove?
options: Control of the private key without sending a transaction or paying gas
questions.explanation: It is the basis of Sign-In With Ethereum.

questions.question: What does verifying a contract on Etherscan do?
options: Publishes the source so it can be matched against the deployed bytecode and read publicly
questions.explanation: Verification gives transparency but is not an audit.

questions.question: Explain reentrancy WITHOUT using the word 'recursive'. Describe how an attacker exploits it and how checks-effects-interactions prevents it.
rubric: Explains that an external call hands control to another contract before state is updated (3)
Describes the attacker's fallback/receive re-entering the vulnerable function (3)
Correctly explains CEI ordering: update state before external interaction (2)
Mentions a second defense such as ReentrancyGuard (1)
Gives a concrete example such as the DAO hack or a vault withdraw (1)

questions.question: Walk through what happens from the moment you click 'Confirm' in MetaMask to the moment your transaction is finalized.
rubric: Transaction is signed locally and broadcast to a node (2)
Enters the mempool and is picked by a block builder based on fees (2)
Included in a block and executed by the EVM, with state changes and gas used (2)
Receipt/logs produced and confirmations accumulate (2)
Finality via PoS attestations and checkpoints (2)

questions.question: Why would a protocol use a proxy pattern, and what are the risks? Mention at least one proxy type.
rubric: Upgradeability: logic can change while address and state are preserved (2)
Explains delegatecall and storage living in the proxy (3)
Names a pattern such as Transparent, UUPS or Beacon (1)
Risks: storage collisions, uninitialized implementation, admin key compromise, selector clashes (3)
Mentions timelocks/multisig/governance as mitigation (1)

questions.question: Explain impermanent loss using a numeric example with a 50/50 ETH/USDC pool.
rubric: Defines IL as the difference versus holding (2)
Uses a correct numeric example, e.g. ETH price doubling gives about 5.7% IL (4)
Explains the AMM rebalancing mechanism as the cause (2)
Explains how fees can offset IL (2)

questions.question: What is the difference between push and pull payments, and why are pull payments generally safer?
rubric: Push means the contract sends funds to recipients; pull means recipients claim them (3)
Push risks include DoS from a reverting recipient and unbounded loops (3)
Push risks include reentrancy and gas griefing (2)
Gives an example implementation such as a withdrawals mapping (2)

questions.question: List and explain at least four best practices for securing an upgradeable smart contract system.
rubric: Multisig/timelock on upgrade authority (2)
Initializer protection and _disableInitializers (2)
Storage layout discipline, gaps, EIP-1967 slots (2)
Testing upgrades and using OpenZeppelin upgrade plugins (2)
Access control, monitoring/pausing, audits (2)

questions.question: Give at least four concrete techniques to reduce gas in a Solidity contract and explain why each works.
rubric: Storage packing (2)
calldata instead of memory, and caching storage reads in memory (2)
immutable/constant and custom errors (2)
Avoiding unbounded loops, unchecked math where safe, events instead of storage (2)
Explanations tie back to EVM costs (2)

questions.question: Review this contract. List every vulnerability, explain how it would be exploited, and give a fix for each.
rubric: withdraw(): reentrancy because state is updated after the external call; fix with CEI or a guard (3)
withdraw(): the ok return value is not checked (1)
sweep(): no access control, so anyone can drain the vault; fix with onlyOwner (3)
setOwner(): no access control; also owner is never set in a constructor (2)
Mentions transfer() gas stipend or adds events/tests as extra credit (1)

questions.question: Explain how a constant-product AMM prices a trade, and why a pool cannot be fully drained by traders.
rubric: States x * y = k and that the trade must keep k constant (3)
Shows how the price moves as reserves change (2)
Explains that draining one reserve requires infinite input of the other, because the price approaches infinity (3)
Mentions slippage/price impact and the effect of fees (2)
